Need to search first.Now fetch full pages.I've written verse-by-verse notes on Judges 18 below, but they are thinner than you asked for. After my first searches I hit the tool limit and couldn't open any full pages. Everything here comes from the search-result text of each page, so some verses have only one or two notes and several sites I intended to check aren't covered at all. These include Gill's and Ellicott's full Judges 18 pages, NET Bible notes, Bible Odyssey, catholic.com, oca.org, Wesley's notes and the Lutheran and Pentecostal denominational sites.

A note on who said what: BibleHub's single-verse pages combine several commentaries, and the text I saw didn't always label each section. Where I name a commentator from those pages, I'm inferring it from the wording, and I say so.

---

**v. 1**
- **Traditional reading:** Guzik says Dan was given land, but they found their own land too hard to conquer. He sees chapter 17 as a few people's private sins, and chapter 18 as those sins spreading to a whole tribe. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-18/
- The Pulpit Commentary says this doesn't mean all of Dan was still without land. The bulk of the tribe, as we read in Joshua 19:40-48, did receive their inheritance by lot before the death of Joshua, but while any part of the tribe was unsettled, the tribe as a whole was still looking. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/judges/18.htm
- Gill takes "no king" to mean no judge or ruler at all. He dates the story after Joshua's death and before Othniel, the first judge, and says the Danites' idolatry led to Israel's later servitude to Cushan-rishathaim. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/18-1.htm
- A Precept Austin devotional note applies it this way: Dan failed to rely on God's power to take its land, and believers who fail to take hold of what God has given them may be starting a spiritual decline. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/60762/
- **Modern scholarship:** The Cambridge Bible points out that Jdg 5:17 implies that Dan was already established in its northern home at the time of Deborah, so this story must come from early in the period. It treats "fallen" (as in allotted by lot) as obviously the comment of a later hand. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/judges/18.htm

**v. 2**
- Keil and Delitzsch (quoted on Precept Austin) read "from their clans" as meaning the spies were sent on behalf of the whole tribe. https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_18_commentary

**v. 3**
- Guzik says the spies may have known the Levite personally, or simply recognized his accent as being from the southern part of Judea. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-18/
- JFB gives the same two options: an old acquaintance, or his regional dialect. https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/judges/18.htm

**v. 4**
- Precept Austin quotes Spurgeon: The man who had already sold himself was easily bought. https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_18_commentary

**v. 5**
- Guzik says this shows what a spiritually confused time this was in Israel. The tribe was on a sinful mission, asked a sinful Levite, and wanted a righteous God to approve it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-18/
- JFB notes the Danites weren't shocked that a Levite was acting as priest or that there was a rival shrine to Shiloh. They were willing to ask the household idols for guidance that could lawfully come only through the high priest's Urim. https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/judges/18.htm
- Pett notices that the Danites say "God" here. He thinks the writer avoided the name Yahweh because their venture broke the covenant. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/judges-18.html

**v. 6** (a point where the commentators really disagree)
- **Most commentators:** JFB calls the answer delusive, and really as ambiguous as those of the heathen oracles. https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/judges/18.htm
- Pett says the writer has already warned readers not to take the answer at face value. There was no way in which this was God's doing. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/judges-18.html
- Precept Austin says the "prophecy" came true only because Dan was strong and Laish was weak. If Dan had really wanted God's advice, they could have asked the high priest at Shiloh. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/60762/
- **Pulpit Commentary (sermon outlines):** A prayer for success that doesn't submit to God's will doesn't justify what you're doing. Prayer cannot sanctify a bad action. It also says success is no proof of God's favour. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/judges-18.html
- **Methodist (Adam Clarke) dissents:** Because the oracle came true, Clarke thinks it a strong presumption that the worship established by Micah was not of an idolatrous kind. He calls it "begging the question" to say the answer was a trick or from the devil. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/clarke/judges/18.htm
- A note on the BibleHub v. 26 page makes a related warning: when things go well for people in their own delusions, they easily conclude that God is pleased with them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/18-26.htm

**v. 7**
- Guzik says Laish was held by a colony of Sidonians, and God had told Israel to drive them out (Joshua 13:4). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-18/
- Clarke thinks Laish was probably a Sidonian colony. Because it was far from Sidon, the Danites could strike before help arrived. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/clarke/judges/18.htm
- Guzik's chapter summary mentions Spurgeon's sermon "Danger of Carnal Security," which used the people of Laish as a picture of false security: no inner struggle, no conscience, no ties to others and no fear. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-18/
- The Pulpit Commentary calls the rest of the verse "exceedingly obscure." It suggests some of the wording may be a quotation from a poem, which would explain the odd grammar. It also reports Robinson identifying Laish with Tell el-Kady, by a great spring that feeds the Jordan. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/judges/18-7.html

**vv. 8–10**
- Keil and Delitzsch (on Precept Austin) take "Why would you fail to act?" as rebuking people sitting idle (1 Kings 22:3). https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/60762/
- Precept Austin says the claim that God had given them the land rested on an oracle that was sought almost as an afterthought and was acquired from a rogue pseudo priest at an idolatrous shrine! https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_18_commentary
- **Modern scholarship:** The Cambridge Bible finds the spies' speech jumbled. It explains this, following Moore, as two stories woven together. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/judges/18.htm

**v. 11**
- Guzik finds it ironic that Dan could raise 600 armed men for Laish but wouldn't fight for its own allotted land. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-18/

**v. 12**
- Pett says Mahaneh-dan means "camp of Dan." It is where the Spirit first stirred Samson (Judges 13:25), perhaps because Samson remembered this great journey of his ancestors. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/judges-18.html

**v. 14**
- The Pulpit Commentary says "in these houses" shows that Micah's house was really a small village (see v. 22). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/judges/18-14.html

**vv. 15–18**
- JFB describes the plan as robbery: the armed men guarded the gate while the five spies plundered the shrine and bribed the priest. It calls the theft a curious medley of low morality and strong religious feeling. https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/judges/18.htm
- Guzik says the priest let it happen by standing aside. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-18/
- Precept Austin quotes Spurgeon: "How insane a thing, that men should steal what they had worshipped, and afterwards worship what they stole." https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_18_commentary
- Pett thinks the priest really was surprised in v. 18. He says repeating the list of objects stresses what the Danites were after and how sacrilegious it was. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/judges-18.html

**v. 19**
- Poole and Gill say "put your hand over your mouth" means keep silent (Job 21:5; 29:9). Gill adds that the Danites wanted the priest as well as the idols because they didn't know how to use the idols without him. He notes it seems to have been common then to call a priest "father." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/18-19.htm

**v. 20**
- The Pulpit Commentary says hopes of more honour and more money stifled all sentiments of gratitude and loyalty to Micah. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/judges/18.htm
- Guzik calls this "mercenary ambition." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-18/
- JFB thinks the priest's place "in the midst of the people" probably copied the place of the priests and the ark in the wilderness marches. https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/judges/18.htm
- Precept Austin quotes Trapp, who cites Luther's advice that preachers keep three "dogs" out of the pulpit: ambition, covetousness and envy. https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_18_commentary

**v. 21**
- Barnes says they expected Micah to chase them and arranged their march to match. Gill says bringing their families and goods shows they never meant to return. Keil and Delitzsch say "the little ones" includes women as well as children. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/18-21.htm

**vv. 22–24**
- Guzik sees strong irony here: Micah had to rescue his own gods. Idol worship can be just a way of worshipping ourselves. A priest who can be taken away points by contrast to Christ, the High Priest who can never be taken from us. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-18/
- Precept Austin: Idolaters worship gods they can carry, but Christians worship a God who carries them! https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_18_commentary
- The Pulpit Commentary (sermon outline) says Micah was wrong to think he would lose God's presence by losing his images. God dwells in the shrine of the heart. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/judges-18.html
- **Methodist (Clarke) dissents:** He holds that Micah worshipped the true God. So "my gods" can't mean idols; it means symbols of the divine presence, such as the teraphim and ephod. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/clarke/judges/18.htm
- **Modern scholarship:** The Cambridge Bible says the phrase could be translated "my God" and that Micah worshipped the LORD. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/judges/18.htm

**vv. 25–26**
- Guzik says this was simply "might makes right." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-18/
- The Cambridge Bible: The rough humour and insolence of the robbers are admirably described. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/judges/18.htm
- Precept Austin says Micah turned around from the Danites when he should have turned around, in repentance, to the LORD. https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_18_commentary

**vv. 27–28**
- The Pulpit Commentary thinks repeating "quiet and secure" shows the writer condemning the deed as cruel, like the slaughter by Simeon and Levi at Shechem. It also says "beside Beth-rehob" means the valley belonged to the Syrians of Beth-rehob (2 Samuel 10:6). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/judges/18.htm and https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/judges-18.html
- A source quoted on Precept Austin says there was no harm in wanting more territory, but readers can only feel horror at wholesale extermination. Consciences trained by Christ are more sensitive than people's were in those rough times. https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_18_commentary

**v. 29**
- Guzik and Clarke both note that "from Dan to Beersheba" became the phrase for the whole land, north to south. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-18/
- The Catholic Encyclopedia says Dan was originally Laish (or Leshem) and was renamed after the 600 Danites destroyed and rebuilt it. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/04615c.htm

**v. 30**
- **Moses or Manasseh:** The Pulpit Commentary says a small letter *nun* was written above the line so the name would be read "Manasseh." That way readers could avoid saying aloud that a descendant of Moses was an idolatrous priest. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/judges/18.htm
- Clarke and Barnes agree that "Moses" is the right reading. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/clarke/judges/18.htm and https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/18-30.htm
- Gill thinks Jonathan was probably Moses' grandson, a contemporary of Aaron's grandson Phinehas. He also allows that other men named Gershom and Manasseh might be meant. (The section reads like Gill.) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/18-30.htm
- A BibleHub Q&A page argues the suspended letter shows careful copying by the scribes, not a contradiction. https://biblehub.com/q/is_jonathan's_lineage_in_judges_18_30_accurate.htm
- **Catholic:** The Catholic Encyclopedia says the Vulgate's "Moses" is the correct reading. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/09583c.htm
- **"The captivity of the land":** The Pulpit Commentary reports two views. Many take it to mean the Assyrian exile. Kimchi and others take it to mean the Philistines capturing the ark in Eli's day, which fits v. 31. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/judges/18.htm
- The Geneva Bible notes (Reformed) take it as the time the ark was captured. They add that the Danites credited their victory to their idols rather than giving God the glory. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/18-30.htm
- Keil and Delitzsch, following Hengstenberg, also link it to the Philistine period. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/18-31.htm
- **The Church Fathers and Dan:** A note on the BibleHub v. 30 page says The Fathers thought, for this reason, that Antichrist would spring from the tribe of Dan. I couldn't see which commentator wrote it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/18-30.htm
- Precept Austin lists the same idea but marks it "not a certainty." It also links Dan's idolatry to the tribe being left out of the list in Revelation 7. https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_18_commentary

**v. 31**
- Guzik calls this the start of *official* idolatry in Israel, a rival to the house of God at Shiloh, and it all began with a son stealing 1,100 shekels. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-18/
- JFB says Dan's distance from Shiloh was their excuse and kept the idolatry going for generations. https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/judges/18.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary suggests this long-running worship explains why Jeroboam later chose Dan for a golden calf. The Catholic Encyclopedia makes the same link. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/18-30.htm and https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/04615c.htm
- Pett suggests Micah's image may have been a small copy of the ark. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/judges-18.html
- GotQuestions says the story shows the result of worshipping by what we think is best rather than according to God's teachings. https://www.gotquestions.org/Micah-idol-Judges.html
- **Methodist (Clarke) dissents:** He calls the Danites properly the first dissenters from the public established worship of the Jews. He doubts they should be called idolaters and thinks this worship was better than having none at all. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/clarke/judges/18.htm
- **Modern scholarship:** The Cambridge Bible thinks v. 31 was not written by the same hand as v. 30. The double ending may be the conclusions of two combined stories. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/judges/18.htm

---

**Where the traditions differ:** The clearest split I found was Adam Clarke, a Methodist. He reads Micah's and Dan's worship as unlawful worship of the true God, not idolatry. Reformed (Geneva), Baptist (Gill, Spurgeon), Guzik (enduringword.com) and most others treat it as idolatry. I found no Lutheran or Pentecostal sources, and no prosperity or word-of-faith teaching on this chapter. The Pulpit Commentary's point that success doesn't prove God's favour is relevant to those debates, but it doesn't mention them.
